analysis.one_liner: Erases air-toxics limits on cement plants and orders EPA to write weaker, slower replacement rules.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on it: with 16 cosponsors (14 Republicans, 2 Democrats), the bill sat in the Environment and Public Works Committee until the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have thrown out the EPA's 2010 rule that limits mercury and other toxic air pollution from cement kilns, along with related waste-burning rules as they apply to cement plants, treating those rules as if they never existed [S3]. It would have ordered EPA to write replacement rules, but barred any compliance deadline sooner than five years after the new rules were final, and required EPA to choose the least burdensome option it legally could [S2]. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Cement plant owners. The 2010 EPA rule required them to install pollution controls to cut mercury, acid gases, and fine particles from their kilns; this bill would have erased those requirements and pushed compliance years into the future [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Voids the 2010 National Emission Standards for Portland cement plants and related solid waste incineration rules as applied to cement, treating them as though they had never taken effect.
Requires EPA to set replacement compliance dates no earlier than five years after new rules are finalized, after weighing costs, feasibility, equipment availability, and potential employment impacts.
Lets the Administrator extend the 15-month deadline for replacement rules to a later date of its own choosing.

Directs EPA to impose the least burdensome regulatory alternative for each replacement rule and to ensure standards can be met under actual operating conditions, reflecting industry arguments that the 2010 rule was unworkable in practice.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near cement kilns, especially children, would breathe mercury, acid gases, and fine particles for years longer. Mercury also settles into water and accumulates in fish, so exposure reaches people well beyond the plant fence line.

drawbacks.text: Nullifying the 2010 rule would have left nearby communities exposed to mercury and other hazardous air pollutants during the entire re-rule period, plus at least five more years before full compliance.
Mandating the least burdensome alternative could push EPA below the level of protection the Clean Air Act health standards would otherwise require.
Defining compliance around cost, equipment availability, and employment impacts, with a five-year minimum, prioritizes industry economics over the health-based deadlines the existing rule set.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits flow to one industry: avoided spending on pollution controls. The costs fall on the public as years of additional mercury and toxic air exposure near roughly a hundred cement plants. This is a delay bill by design — it does not repeal pollution control permanently, but it would have pushed the protections back most of a decade.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in September 2011, and that is the last thing that ever happened to it; it died there when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Barrasso introduced the Cement Sector Regulatory Relief Act on September 22, 2011, with original cosponsors including Sens. Manchin, Blunt, and Landrieu.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded.
It attracted 16 cosponsors, 14 Republicans and 2 Democrats.
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and all bills not passed die with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People living near cement plants are better off: the EPA's 2010 mercury and air-toxics limits stayed in effect instead of being wiped out and replaced on a five-year-plus delay. The cement industry did not get the relief it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near cement plants, not the industry

sides.party_line_note: Fourteen of the bill's 16 cosponsors were Republicans; two Democrats (Manchin and Landrieu) joined. The Democratic committee chair never moved it, and no vote ever took place.

industries.note: The bill voids the 2010 rule requiring cement kilns to cut mercury, acid gases, and particulate emissions, sparing the industry the cost of installing pollution controls. Those avoided costs are paid by the public as years of additional toxic air exposure near the plants.

By delaying and lightening the emission standards, the bill would defer demand for the scrubbers, filters, and monitoring equipment cement plants would otherwise have had to buy. Its interest runs with the public's interest in cleaner air.
